column2: Thinking himself rebuked, the Magadhan, knowing it to be true, honoured him with folded hands.
Arjuna, consoling him, said again: "You should come on the full moon of Chaitra to our king's horse sacrifice."
Thus addressed, Sahadeva's son, saying "So be it," duly honoured that horse and Phalguna, best of warriors.
Then the lion-like one went on as he wished, and along the sea-shore to the Vangas, Pundras and Keralas.
Here and there, many armies of barbarians were conquered by Dhananjaya with the Gandiva bow, O king.
Then the horse, turning back, strong and going at will, reached the lovely city of the Chedis called Shuktisahvaya.
It was honoured there by Sharabha, son of Shishupala, with pride after battle and with worship.
Honoured there, king, the best of horses went on to the Kashis, Andhras, Kosalas, Kiratas and Tanganas.
Receiving worship there as is fit, the Pandava, son of Kunti, turned back and went to the Dasharnas.
There a mighty lord of the earth named Chitrangada fought Vijaya in a most terrible battle.
Having brought him under control too, the bull among men, Kirithin, went to the land of the Nishada king Ekalavya.
Ekalavya's son seized the horse in battle, and he made a hair-raising war with the Nishadas.
Then Kunti's son, unconquered in battles, the hero, conquered him too in the fight, as he was raised to obstruct the sacrifice.
There too, with Dravidas, Andhras, Raudras, Mahishakas, and with Kollagireyas, Kirithin had a battle.
Then, under the horse's lead, he went all round Surashtra and, reaching Gokarna, went also to Prabhasa.
Then the glorious sacrificial horse of the Kuru king reached lovely Dvaravati, guarded by the Vrishni heroes.
The Yadava boys, harassing the best of horses, set out against it, and then Ugrasena stopped them, O king.
Then the lord of the Vrishnis and Andhakas came out of the city with Vasudeva, Kirithin's maternal uncle.
Meeting the best of the Kurus rightly and lovingly, they honoured the best of the Bharatas with great worship; and with their leave he went where the horse had gone.
Then the horse in due course roamed the western region of the sea and then went to the rich Panchanada.
From there too, Kaurava, the horse roamed the land of Gandhara as it wished, followed by Kunti's son.
There a terrible battle took place with the king of Gandhara, Shakuni's son, following old enmity.
Unable to bear the killing of King Shakuni, those warriors came together against Partha with bows drawn.
The righteous, unconquered Bibhatsu told them Yudhishthira's words, but they did not take the good counsel.
Though restrained by Partha with conciliation, they were angered and surrounded the horse; then the Pandava grew angry.
Then the Pandava cut off their heads with razor-heads loosed from Gandiva, blazing at the tips, with no great effort, as with Jayadratha's head.
Struck by Partha, they let go the horse in confusion and turned back, O great king, greatly afflicted by showers of arrows.
Though pierced by those Gandharas, the best of the Pandavas, radiant, singling them out, felled their heads.
While the Gandharas were being slain on every side in the fight, the king, Shakuni's son, stood against the Pandava.
To that king fighting, standing in kshatriya dharma, Partha said: "Kings are not to be killed by me by the king's order. Enough of fighting, hero; you have no defeat today."
Partha, unflustered, took off his helmet with a crescent arrow, as with Jayadratha's head.
Seeing that, all the Gandharas were amazed; they knew the king had not been killed because he did not wish it.
Shakuni's son, seeking a moment to flee, shone with those same frightened ones like small deer.
Of those running about right there, Partha swiftly took heads with bent-jointed broad-headed arrows.
Some did not notice their raised arms struck off by broad arrows loosed from Gandiva and urged by Partha.
That army, its men, elephants and horses bewildered, broke and rallied again and again, mostly slain and shattered.
Before that hero of foremost deeds no enemies were seen who could withstand his great arrows as they were felled.
Then the mother of the Gandhara king, afraid, came out with aged ministers in front, bearing the best guest-offering.
Unflustered, she held back her son, mad for battle, and appeased Jishnu, who does not toil.
Honouring her, Kunti's son showed grace then, and consoling Shakuni's son said this:

It does not please me, mighty-armed slayer of foes, that you formed this resolve to fight me; you are my very brother, blameless one.
mahabharata:14:85.22	Remembering my mother Gandhari and what Dhritarashtra did, you live, king, though your followers were slain.
mahabharata:14:85.23	Do not do so; let enmity be calmed; let not such a thought be yours; come on the full moon of Chaitra to our king's horse sacrifice.
Yudhishthira heard through a spy that he had turned back, and hearing that Arjuna was well, he was glad in mind.
Hearing of Vijaya's deed in the Gandhara land and in other lands too, the king was greatly pleased.
Meanwhile, on the twelfth of the fortnight of Magha, taking a favourable star, the king of dharma Yudhishthira,
the greatly radiant, great-minded one, summoned all his brothers: Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva, Kaurava.
The best of those who uphold dharma, best of speakers, said these words at the proper time to Bhima of terrible valour.

Bhimasena, your younger brother is coming with the horse, as my men who follow Dhananjaya say.
mahabharata:14:86.8	This is the time that has come; the horse is on all sides; this is Magha's full moon, and the month has just a little left, Vrikodara.
mahabharata:14:86.9	So let learned brahmins, Veda-masters, be sent to examine a place fit for the sacrifice, for the success of the horse sacrifice.
Then Bhimasena went with wise builders, putting brahmins skilled in sacrificial rites in front.
The Kaurava had the sacrificial ground measured by rule, a village with sala trees, roads and gates.
He had made, by rule, a hall, a house for the wife, the Agnidhra, and the northern altar, adorned with jewels and gold.
He set pillars adorned with gold and great gateways in the sacrificial precincts, and gave pure gold.
The righteous one had made the women's apartments for kings from various lands here and there by rule.
And Bhima had made various houses for brahmins who had come from many lands, in many ways.
By the king's command, Bhimasena sent messengers to the kings of untroubled deeds.
Those best of kings came for the pleasure of the lord of the Kurus, bringing many jewels, women, horses and weapons.
As they settled in thousands of those camps, the roar, like the roaring sea, seemed to touch the sky.
For those who came, the lotus-eyed king ordered food, drink and beds, more than human.
He, king of dharma, ordered many stalls for vehicles, filled with rice and milk products, tiger among men.
At that great sacrifice of the wise king of dharma many hosts of sages, speakers of Brahman, assembled.
And the best of the twice-born who were there assembled with their pupils, and the Kaurava received them.
Yudhishthira himself, the greatly radiant, giving up pride, followed them all as far as their lodgings.
Then the builders and the other craftsmen reported to the king of dharma the whole arrangement of the sacrifice.
Hearing that all was done, the faultless king of dharma, with his brothers, was glad.
The kings saw the chief arrangement of the sacrifice, made by Bhima like Indra's, delight of the Kurus.
They saw gateways of gold, and very many beds, seats and pleasure-grounds adorned with jewels.
Jars, dishes, cauldrons, pitchers and vessels: the kings saw nothing there that was not of gold.
Sacrificial posts as the scriptures say, of wood adorned with gold, were duly set up in time, very radiant.
Whatever animals there were, of land and water, lord, those kings saw them all brought together.
Cows, buffaloes, aged women, creatures of the water, beasts of prey and birds,
womb-born, egg-born, sweat-born and sprout-born beings, wild creatures of mountains and marshes, they saw.
Seeing the sacrificial ground so completely delighted with animals, cattle, wealth and grain, the kings came to great wonder; much refined food for brahmins and vaishyas, abundant.
It roared again and again, day by day; so that sacrifice of the wise king of dharma went on.
They saw, king, many mountain-like heaps of food, canals of curds and lakes of ghee.
The whole of Jambudvipa, with many countries and peoples, seemed, O king, gathered in one place at that great sacrifice of the king.
There, thousands of kinds of men from here and there came, taking wealth, many, bull of the Bharatas.
Kings, garlanded, with well-polished jewelled earrings, served the best of the twice-born by hundreds and thousands.
The followers of the kings gave to brahmins various foods and drinks that were fit for kings' enjoyment.
These tigers among men have come, the lords of the world; let honour be made to them, for kings are worthy of honour.
So addressed by the renowned king, the greatly radiant Bhimasena did so with the twins, O Bharata.
Then Govinda came, best of all living beings, with the Vrishnis to the son of Dharma, putting Baladeva first.
He came with Yuyudhana, Pradyumna, Gada, Nishatha, Samba and Kritavarma.
The mighty-armed Bhima paid them supreme honour, and those bulls among men entered jewelled houses.
In Yudhishthira's presence, at the end of the tales, Madhusudana spoke of Arjuna, much worn by many battles.
The king of dharma asked him again and again about his brother, scourge of foes, and the lord of the world told it.

A man of mine from Dvaraka came, king, who saw the best of the Pandavas worn by many battles.
mahabharata:14:88.11	Thus addressed, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, replied: By good fortune Jishnu is well and is coming, Madhava.
I wish you, delight of the Yadus, to tell me what that foremost of the Pandava force instructed."
Thus addressed, O tiger among kings, the lord of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, eloquent, said this to the righteous Yudhishthira.

Partha, the man, said this, great king: 'Let Yudhishthira be told by me, Krishna, this word of mine at the proper time.
mahabharata:14:88.15	Kings will come from every side to the Kauravas; each one of them is to be honoured; that is fitting for us.
mahabharata:14:88.16	By this word the king should be informed on my behalf, giver of honour; there should be no delay in bringing guest-offerings.
mahabharata:14:88.17	The king should do it, and you should consent; through king's hatred these subjects would not perish again, O king.
mahabharata:14:88.18	And, son of Kunti, that man said another word of Dhananjaya's; hear what I tell, O king.
mahabharata:14:88.19	The lord of Manipura will come to our sacrifice, my son, the greatly radiant, dear Babhruvahana.
mahabharata:14:88.20	You should honour him by rule out of regard for me, for he is always devoted and attached to me, lord.'
Hearing these words, Yudhishthira, king of dharma, welcomed his speech and said this.

I have heard, Hrishikesha, that Vijaya fought many battles again with kings, here and there.
mahabharata:14:89.3	Because of me Partha is always without happiness; my mind grieves that the wise Vijaya suffers so much.
mahabharata:14:89.4	I think always in private about Kunti's son, Vrishni: what bad mark is there in his body, honoured with all marks, by which he meets sorrows, Krishna?
mahabharata:14:89.5	Kunti's son always shares in great sorrow; yet I do not see any blameworthy mark on Bibhatsu's limbs. If this should be heard by me, you should tell it.
Thus addressed, Hrishikesha, increaser of the Bhojas, after reflecting a long while, said to the king:

I do not see, O king, any bad mark in him, except that the shins of the lion among men are too long.
mahabharata:14:89.8	By those that tiger among men is always joined to journeys; I see nothing else by which Jaya shares in sorrow.
So told truly by the wise Krishna, the best of the Kurus said to the tiger of the Vrishnis, "So it is, lord."
But Krishna Draupadi looked at Krishna sideways with envy; and the slayer of Keshi accepted her love, the friend of friend Hrishikesha, as if Dhananjaya himself.
There Bhima and the Kurus and the Yadavas rejoiced hearing the varied tales of Dhananjaya, lord.
As they spoke so, tales of Arjuna, a man came with word of the great-souled Vijaya.
The wise one approached the best of the Kurus, saluted him, and reported that the tiger among men Arjuna had come.
Hearing that, the king, his eyes full of tears of joy, gave him much wealth for the good tidings.
Then on the second day a great sound grew as the Pandavas' burden-bearer, tiger among men, was coming.
Then dust rose, and the horse as it moved about shone like Ucchaihshravas.
There Arjuna heard the joyful words of men: "By good fortune you are well, Partha; blessed is King Yudhishthira.
Who else but Arjuna, having conquered the whole earth with its kings and led the best of horses about, would come back?
Of the great-souled kings of old, Sagara and the rest, we have heard of no such deed.
What you, best of the Kurus, have done here, so hard, other future kings will not do."
Hearing such words pleasant to the ear from those people speaking, the righteous Phalguna entered the sacrificial enclosure.
Then the king with his ministers and Krishna, delight of the Yadus, putting Dhritarashtra first, went to meet him.
He saluted the feet of his father, the wise king of dharma, and honoured Bhima and the rest, and embraced Keshava.
Met and honoured by them, he honoured them in return by rule, and the righteous one rested, like one who has gained the shore.
At that very time King Babhruvahana, the wise one, came to the Kurus with his two mothers.
Meeting all the Kurus and welcomed by them all, he entered the best house of his grandmother Kunti.
So too the goddess Chitrangada, and the Kaurava's daughter Ulupi, went humbly together to Pritha and Krishna, and to Subhadra and the other Kuru women, as is fit.
Kunti then gave them various jewels, and Draupadi, Subhadra and the other women gave too.
Those two goddesses stayed there on greatly valuable beds and seats, honoured by Kunti herself out of wish to please Partha.
And the greatly valiant, honoured King Babhruvahana waited on King Dhritarashtra by rule.
Approaching King Yudhishthira and the Pandavas Bhima and the rest, the greatly radiant one saluted them humbly.
Embraced by them with love and honoured by rule, those great chariot-fighters, pleased, gave him much wealth.
So too that king humbly attended Krishna, bearer of discus and mace, as Pradyumna attends Govinda.
Krishna gave that king a highly valued, honoured chariot adorned with gold and yoked with divine horses.
Then on the third day the sage, Satyavati's son, approaching Yudhishthira, said eloquently:

From today, son of Kunti, sacrifice; for the time is yours; the auspicious hour has come and the priests urge you.
mahabharata:14:90.13	This sacrifice of yours, king of kings, is the Ahina, with its options; from the abundance of gold it is called Bahusuvarnaka.
mahabharata:14:90.14	Even so, great king, give a threefold fee; let it go to a threefold; for the brahmins are the cause here.
mahabharata:14:90.15	Having performed three horse sacrifices here with many fees, you will cast off the sin done by the killing of kin, lord of men.
mahabharata:14:90.16	This is supreme purity and the purest of purifiers, since you, delight of the Kurus, will gain the closing bath of the horse sacrifice.
Thus addressed by Vyasa of immeasurable radiance, the righteous, radiant king entered the consecration to gain the horse sacrifice, and performed the great horse sacrifice.
There the Veda-knowing priests, O king, performed the rites, circling, knowing the scriptures, rightly well trained.
There was no stumbling among them nor any wrong offering; the best of brahmins did what was proper and in order.
Having properly performed the Pravargya, the righteous best of the twice-born, O king, then performed the pressing by rule.
Having pressed the soma, O king, the best of soma-drinkers performed the pressings in order, following the scriptures.
There was no miserable man, no poor man, no hungry or suffering person, nor even a common man there.
The greatly radiant Bhimasena constantly had food given to those wanting food, by the king's command.
The priests skilled in the arrangement performed all the rites day by day, eyes on the meaning of the scriptures.
There was no member of his assembly who did not know the limbs of the rite, none without vows, none without a teacher, no brahmin unable to debate.
Then when the time came to raise the posts, O best of the Bharatas, there were six of bilva, as many of khadira, equal to bilva, and as many of every kind.
Two posts of the lord of the Kurus were made of deodar, and the priests had one made of shleshmataka.
For beauty, bull among men, Bhima had other golden posts made by the king of dharma's command.
They shone, royal sage, decked with garments, like the seven sages in heaven who have come to the gods.
Golden bricks were made there for the fire-altar, and the altar there shone like that of Daksha Prajapati.
It was four-layered, eighteen cubits, with golden wings, three-fold, in the form of a garuda.
Then animals were appointed by the wise as the scriptures say, to each god, birds and beasts.
Bulls as the scriptures say and water creatures: all these they consecrated there in the rite of building the altar.
At the posts were fixed three hundred animals, with the horse as the best, for the great soul, the king, Kunti's son.
That sacrifice shone, crowded with divine sages in person, filled with hosts of gandharvas and adorned with hosts of apsarases.
It was adorned with the songs of kimpurushas and kinnaras, and surrounded on all sides by dwellings of perfected brahmins.
In that assembly were always Vyasa's pupils, best of the twice-born, authors of all the scriptures, skilled in sacrificial rites.
Narada was there, and Tumburu of great radiance, Vishvavasu, Chitrasena and other knowers of song.
Gandharvas skilled in song and expert in dance delighted those brahmins in the intervals of the sacrificial rites.
Then, having rightly slaughtered the horse, the best of priests made the daughter of Drupada, the high-minded, lie down by it, by rule, with three Kalas, O king.
Having taken out its fat as the scriptures say, the best of the twice-born cooked it unflustered, as the scriptures say, O best of the Bharatas.
The king of dharma with his brothers duly smelled the smoke of that fat, which removes all sin.
The remaining limbs of that horse, O king, were offered into the fire by all sixteen priests, the steadfast.
Having completed that sacrifice of the king of Indra-like radiance, the blessed Vyasa with his pupils increased the king.
Then Yudhishthira gave by rule to the members of the assembly a thousand crores of nishkas, and the earth to Vyasa.
Accepting the earth, O king, Vyasa, Satyavati's son, said to the best of the Bharatas, the righteous Yudhishthira:
This earth, best of kings, is entrusted by you to these; let a price be given to me, for brahmins desire wealth.

I shall enter the forest, lords of brahmins; divide this earth, making the earth into four parts by the measure of the four priests.
mahabharata:14:91.13	I do not wish to take brahmins' property, best of sages; this is my constant view and my brothers', blameless ones.
When he had said this, his brothers and Draupadi said, "So it is," and that was hair-raising.
Then a voice in the sky said "Well done, well done," O Bharata, and the sound of brahmin hosts praising it shone.
Dvaipayana, thus told, spoke again to Yudhishthira in the midst of brahmins, honouring him:
This earth was given to me by you; I give it back to you. Let gold be given to these twice-born; the earth is yours.
Then Vasudeva said to Yudhishthira, king of dharma: "You should do as the blessed Vyasa says."
So addressed, the best of the Kurus, glad with his brothers, gave a fee three times as great, crores upon crores, for the sacrifice.
No other king will do in the world what was done by the Kuru lion, imitating Marutta.
Taking that wealth, Krishna Dvaipayana the lord gave it to the priests, and the learned ones divided it in four.
Having given that gold as the price of the earth, Yudhishthira, his sins shaken off and heaven conquered, rejoiced with his brothers.
The priests then divided that endless heap of gold among the twice-born as they wished and were able.
Whatever gold there was in the sacrificial ground, ornaments, gateways, posts, pitchers, vessels and bricks, the twice-born divided it all with Yudhishthira's leave.
After the brahmins, kshatriyas took the wealth, and hosts of vaishyas and shudras and other barbarian peoples; in great time they took that gold from here and there.
Then all those brahmins, glad, went to their homes, gratified by that wealth of the great-souled king of dharma.
The blessed greatly radiant Vyasa gave to Kunti, for her saluting his feet, his own share of that great gold.
Receiving that gift of love from her father-in-law, Pritha, pleased in mind, then did great merit in the world.
Having gone to the closing bath, the king, freed from sin with his brothers, shone, honoured, like Mahendra with the gods.
And the Pandavas, surrounded by the assembled kings, shone, great king, like planets among hosts of stars.
Then he gave the kings too various jewels, elephants, horses, ornaments, women, clothes and gold.
Scattering that endless flood of wealth in the circle of kings, King Partha shone like Vaishravana.
Having summoned the hero King Babhruvahana and given him vast wealth, he sent him home.
And that child, Duhshala's grandson, bull among kings, he consecrated lovingly in his own kingdom, guarded by his fathers.
And all those kings, well divided and well honoured, the king of the Kurus, Yudhishthira, sent off, having won them over.
So was the sacrifice of the wise king of dharma, with floods of food, wealth and jewels, and oceans of liquor and maireya.
There, bull of the Bharatas, were mud of ghee, many lakes, mountains of food, mud of rasala and canals.
Eat the dishes, shadava and ragas; let them be made, let them be eaten, and the slaughter of animals: no end was seen there.
Intoxicated, delighted, with young women singing, it was then charming with the sound of drums and conches.
Give, eat, day and night without hindrance; people from various lands told of that like a great festival, crowded with very glad people.
Having rained showers of wealth, with desires, jewels and riches, the best of the Bharatas, freed from sin, his aim fulfilled, entered the city.
You should always protect yourself in meals and the like, with men skilled in matters, known by family and conduct, O Bharata.
The king, Bhimasena, Sahadeva the Pandava, Nakula and Yajnaseni: we six are of one mind.
All this has been told to you, as recited by Vaishampayana, at the command of Vyasa, at the serpent sacrifice of the king.
